To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we screened the PFN1 (profilin-1) gene in a large cohort of patients with sporadic amyotrophy lateral sclerosis and in patients with frontotemporal degeneration and we found only one mutation, the p.E117 G variant, which is likely a less pathogenic mutation according to both frequency and functional experiments.
PFN1 gene mutations are very rare in sporadic ALS cases.
we screened the PFN1 in a large series of sporadic ALS patients and in a panel of control subjects.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular basis underlying ALS and FTD and the characterization of novel genetic risk factors.
the identification of genetic factors involved in the pathogenesis of ALS and FTD.
the screening of PFN gene in sporadic and familial ALS patients and in FTD cases, in order to determine the effective contribution to neurodegeneration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
PFN1 is a gene of low penetrance in ALS, and that it is not a major genetic determinant of the sporadic form of the disease.
PFN1 is a rare cause of SALS and FTD.
PFN1 gene is not a common genetic determinant of SALS or FTD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PFN1 gene mutations are not frequent in SALS and in FTD, but the role of this gene in the etiology of ALS and in the overlap between these 3 diseases remains to be determined.
PFN1 screening is not a routine procedure in SALS and FTD, and it is not necessary to perform PFN1 sequencing for every SALS or FTD patient.
the p.E117K mutation is likely to represent the only pathogenic PFN1 variant in SALS and in FTD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PFN1 should be included in the genetic screening of ALS patients.
PFN1 should not be included among the genes to be sequenced in the diagnostic work-up for SALS.
PFN1 screening is not recommended for SALS and FTD patients.
